clue.text: Might be seen as apt ruler of French fairy tale

definitions.note: the man of the French fairy tale, its author

indicators.note: the letters of the words that follow might be seen in another order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone apt to rule turns up as a figure in a French fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might be seen as' tells you to rearrange APT RULER. Charles Perrault collected Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty, so he is the man 'of French fairy tale'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Perrault was the seventeenth-century French writer who set down Cinderella, Puss in Boots and other classic fairy stories.

clue.text: "… gaily dressed women, all young and beautiful, one of them with a— spaniel upon her lap" (The Poison Belt, A. Conan Doyle)

definitions.text: "… gaily dressed women, all young and beautiful, one of them with a— spaniel upon her lap" (The Poison Belt, A. Conan Doyle)

parts.words: "… gaily dressed women, all young and beautiful, one of them with a— spaniel upon her lap" (The Poison Belt, A. Conan Doyle)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing word is the breed of toy dog, named after the old form of China's capital, that Conan Doyle wrote here

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Conan Doyle's Professor Challenger story: the dog on the lady's lap is a toy spaniel named after the Chinese capital's older spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pekingese, a small lapdog bred at the Chinese imperial court, is often shortened to the city's old name.

clue.text: I grant new measure of TV success

indicators.note: new letters are made from the words before, giving them a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A man boasts that a new measure of how popular TV shows are is his own grant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' tells you to rearrange I GRANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme's viewing figures are its ratings, the number used to judge whether a show has done well.

clue.text: Composer to supplement with marketing?

parts.note: to add in is to supplement, putting something extra in
to sell is the aim of marketing, pushing goods to buyers

explanation.surface: A composer is told to boost his income with some marketing.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Addinsell was the English composer of the Warsaw Concerto. 'to' and 'with' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Addinsell wrote film music, most famously the Warsaw Concerto for Dangerous Moonlight.

clue.text: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing

definitions.text: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing

parts.words: Hotspur would have had his wife emulate her singing
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1, Hotspur teases his wife Kate to sing as Mortimer's Welsh wife has just done

explanation.surface: Hotspur wanted his wife to sing like another noblewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry IV Part 1 (Act III), Glendower's daughter, married to Mortimer, sings in Welsh; Hotspur then asks his own wife Kate for a song, which she refuses.
explanation.definitionFit: Glendower's daughter, wife of Edmund Mortimer, is the Welsh-speaking lady who sings in that scene.

clue.text: Deity from Le Fanu (bisexual, possibly)

indicators.note: the deity is taken from inside the run of letters in the words after it

explanation.surface: A god appears in a story by Le Fanu, whose characters are possibly bisexual.
explanation.walkthrough: The god hides across 'Fanu bisexual'. 'possibly' is only surface colour: Le Fanu's vampire tale Carmilla is often read as having a bisexual heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead and embalming.

clue.text: Given name of one of many writing in the small back room

definitions.text: Given name of one of many writing in the small back room

parts.words: Given name of one of many writing in the small back room
parts.note: the first name of the novelist who wrote The Small Back Room, a name shared with many other writers

explanation.surface: One of many writers crammed into a small back office is named.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Balchin wrote the novel The Small Back Room (1943); the clue also suggests many writers hunched in a back office.
explanation.definitionFit: Balchin's first name was Nigel, a forename borne by many authors.

clue.text: Rainbow sisters

parts.note: the surname of Ursula and Gudrun, the sisters in D. H. Lawrence's The Rainbow

explanation.walkthrough: The Rainbow is D. H. Lawrence's novel, not the weather: its sisters Ursula and Gudrun share a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen are the sisters at the centre of Lawrence's The Rainbow and Women in Love.

clue.text: Possibly mask this worship of female principle

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of the words that follow could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Perhaps someone hides behind a mask in a cult honouring the feminine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' tells you to rearrange MASK THIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaktism is the Hindu tradition devoted to Shakti, the divine feminine energy.

clue.text: Grasshoppers appearing on Coolidge covers

definitions.meaning: the American green bush-crickets named for their call
Susan Coolidge's books are What Katy Did, What Katy Did at School and What Katy Did Next, so those words appear on their covers

explanation.walkthrough: Coolidge is the children's author Susan Coolidge, not the American president.
explanation.definitionFit: Bush-crickets in America are named for their song, and Susan Coolidge's book titles each print the same two words.

clue.text: Tennessee's nocturnal lizard

parts.note: the reptile in the title of Tennessee Williams's play The Night of the ...

explanation.surface: A lizard from Tennessee comes out at night.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennessee is the playwright Tennessee Williams, not the state; his play is The Night of the Iguana, so the lizard belongs to the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Williams's 1961 play takes its name from a tropical lizard tied up on a hotel veranda.

clue.text: "Three of us have done a— —in Myfleet" (Guilty Thing Surprised, Ruth Rendell)

definitions.text: "Three of us have done a— —in Myfleet" (Guilty Thing Surprised, Ruth Rendell)

parts.words: "Three of us have done a— —in Myfleet" (Guilty Thing Surprised, Ruth Rendell)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the detectives in Rendell's novel have carried out an enquiry calling at every door in the village

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from a Ruth Rendell Wexford novel: police calling at each door in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A door-to-door enquiry, calling at every dwelling in a street, is the police term for this kind of search.

clue.text: Some very thin stuff from French society hostess

definitions.meaning: a sheer lightweight fabric of silk or rayon
... de l'Enclos, the seventeenth-century Parisian courtesan who kept a famous salon

explanation.walkthrough: 'from' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The sheer fabric is a fine voile, and the hostess was Ninon de l'Enclos of seventeenth-century Paris.

clue.text: Depart overnight from Pinter

definitions.meaning: to do a ... flit, slipping away by night to dodge rent
the title of Harold Pinter's 1993 play

explanation.walkthrough: A 'moonlight flit' is British slang for leaving one's lodgings secretly at night without paying; 'from' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave by night to escape creditors is to flit by the moon's light, and Pinter's 1993 play has that title.

clue.text: Strange relatives went hand in hand

definitions.note: a description of those who went hand in hand, not a verb: in Macbeth the witches sing 'The weird sisters, hand in hand'

explanation.surface: Some odd relatives were seen holding hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: Macbeth's witches chant 'The weird sisters, hand in hand, Posters of the sea and land'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's three witches call themselves by this name as they dance in a ring holding hands.

clue.text: Observing rules, like some of Chomsky's strictures

definitions.text: Observing rules, like some of Chomsky's strictures

parts.words: Observing rules, like some of Chomsky's strictures
parts.note: following grammatical rules, and the adjective in the title of Noam Chomsky's 1957 book on structures

explanation.surface: Someone obeys rules as strict as Chomsky's.
explanation.walkthrough: Chomsky's founding book is Syntactic Structures; 'strictures' plays on that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical sentences obey the rules of syntax, and Chomsky's 1957 book names those structures.

clue.text: Random choice of Smollett

parts.note: Tobias Smollett's picaresque hero Random, whose given name is the one wanted

explanation.surface: An arbitrary pick from Smollett's works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Random' is the surname of Smollett's hero, not a sense of 'chance'; his given name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adventures of Roderick Random (1748) is Tobias Smollett's first novel.

clue.text: A poet abbreviates

parts.note: Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate from 1913 to 1930

explanation.surface: A poet trims his verses.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges was a British Poet Laureate.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten a text, cutting it down, is to abridge it.

clue.text: Frank Scott hero, who hardly saw fair service from his employee

definitions.text: Frank Scott hero, who hardly saw fair service from his employee

parts.words: Frank Scott hero, who hardly saw fair service from his employee
parts.note: the narrator of Scott's Rob Roy is Frank, whose servant is named Andrew Fairservice

explanation.surface: A candid hero of Scott got poor service from his man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' is the hero's first name, not 'candid'; his servant in Rob Roy is the unreliable gardener Andrew Fairservice.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Osbaldistone narrates Walter Scott's Rob Roy (1817).

clue.text: Version of the Ring from Maugham?

definitions.meaning: a ring is a circular shape, another name for it
the title of Somerset Maugham's 1921 comedy

explanation.walkthrough: 'the Ring' suggests Wagner, but means only a round band; Maugham's play is The Circle.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring is a round shape, and Somerset Maugham's comedy of 1921 carries that title.

clue.text: Poet reveals masculine type's part in the Mansfield Park ms

indicators.note: the poet is part of the letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: A poet finds a manly character in the manuscript of Mansfield Park.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet's name hides across 'the Mansfield'; it also reads as 'masculine type's' (a he-man's), which the clue's middle states. Felicia Hemans wrote 'Casabianca'.
explanation.definitionFit: Felicia Hemans was the popular early nineteenth-century poet of 'The boy stood on the burning deck'.

clue.text: Trevor's solitary queen?

parts.note: William Trevor's novel ... Alone, whose heroine shares a queen's name

explanation.surface: A queen in Trevor's work rules alone.
explanation.walkthrough: Trevor is the Irish novelist William Trevor; his 1973 novel Elizabeth Alone gives a royal name with 'solitary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two English monarchs bear the name of Trevor's lonely heroine.

clue.text: An opening for novelist

parts.note: a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: A writer gets his first chance.
explanation.walkthrough: James Agate was a drama critic who also wrote novels.
explanation.definitionFit: James Agate, best known as a theatre critic and diarist, published several novels.

clue.text: Eponymous heroine of Bayley and Dodgson

definitions.text: Eponymous heroine of Bayley and Dodgson

parts.words: Eponymous heroine of Bayley and Dodgson
parts.note: John Bayley wrote a novel named after its heroine, and Charles Dodgson (Lewis Carroll) named his Wonderland books after his

explanation.surface: Two authors give their books the name of the heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodgson is Lewis Carroll's real name; John Bayley, Iris Murdoch's husband, published a novel with the same title heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's girl in Wonderland, and Bayley's 1994 novel, share this name in their titles.

clue.text: Monica in some far-reaching ramification of work by Delafield

indicators.note: the surname sits in some of the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman called Monica appears in a far-reaching consequence of a Delafield book.
explanation.walkthrough: Monica's surname hides across 'reaching ramification'; she is the heroine of E. M. Delafield's Thank Heaven Fasting, which 'of work by Delafield' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: Monica Ingram is the debutante heroine of E. M. Delafield's 1932 novel Thank Heaven Fasting.

clue.text: She sadly did not profit from The Return of the Native

definitions.text: She sadly did not profit from The Return of the Native

parts.words: She sadly did not profit from The Return of the Native
parts.note: Hardy's tragic heroine Vye, who gains nothing from Clym Yeobright's homecoming and drowns

explanation.surface: A woman gained nothing from a man coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: The Return of the Native is Hardy's novel, but also the event in it: Clym's return brings Eustacia Vye no escape, only her death.
explanation.definitionFit: Eustacia Vye is the restless heroine of Thomas Hardy's The Return of the Native.

clue.text: Musical fate

definitions.meaning: the 1953 Broadway show set in Baghdad
destiny, a word from Turkish and Arabic

explanation.definitionFit: Destiny is the sense of the Turkish-Arabic loan, and the 1953 Broadway show with Borodin's tunes took it as title.

clue.text: Ushers may form Hera sect

indicators.note: the letters of the words that follow may form something new when rearranged

explanation.surface: Temple attendants might make up a cult of the goddess Hera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may form' tells you to rearrange HERA SECT. An usher is an old word for an assistant schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Usher once meant an under-master in a school, an assistant who taught.
